problem_statement:
LangChain's provider integrations lack consistent, hardened support for secure transport configuration, creating a fragmented and insecure experience for enterprise and security-conscious users. Three categories of failure have been observed across real-world deployments:

First, ChatAnthropic does not accept a custom httpx client, making it impossible to configure mutual TLS (mTLS), certificate-based authentication, or custom SSL settings — capabilities that are table-stakes in enterprise proxy and zero-trust network environments. Multiple teams have reported being fully blocked from using ChatAnthropic in such environments, with no in-product workaround available.

Second, AzureChatOpenAI creates a new httpx connection pool per instance rather than accepting or reusing a shared client, undermining resource efficiency and making it impossible for operators to enforce consistent client lifecycle policy (e.g., pinned certificates or org-wide proxy settings) across all instances in a service.

Third, MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration fails to forward Authorization headers during the discovery phase, resulting in 403 errors when connecting to remote MCP servers that require authentication at the handshake stage — again with no supported workaround.

Finally, the SSRF protection in validate_safe_url can be completely bypassed when the environment variable LANGCHAIN_ENV is set to local_test, allowing attacker-controlled hostnames to skip all URL validation. This represents a security vulnerability that could be exploited in any deployment where that environment variable is present or can be influenced.

Together, these gaps mean that enterprise users cannot adopt key integrations, and that the platform carries an exploitable security regression in its URL validation layer.
target_user: Enterprise software engineers and platform teams deploying LangChain integrations in security-controlled environments — including zero-trust networks, mTLS-enforced infrastructure, and systems with organizational proxy or certificate policies — as well as security engineers responsible for hardening LangChain-based services against SSRF and credential-forwarding vulnerabilities.

user_stories.persona: an enterprise backend engineer deploying ChatAnthropic behind a corporate mTLS proxy
user_stories.action: inject a pre-configured custom httpx client into the ChatAnthropic integration
user_stories.value: I can enforce mutual TLS, certificate-based auth, and SSL customization without patching or monkey-patching the library

user_stories.persona: a platform engineer managing many AzureChatOpenAI instances within a shared service
user_stories.action: supply a single shared httpx client to AzureChatOpenAI at construction time
user_stories.value: all instances share a managed connection pool with consistent certificate pinning and proxy settings, rather than creating redundant pools per instance

user_stories.persona: a developer integrating a remote MCP server that requires an Authorization header during the discovery handshake
user_stories.action: configure Authorization headers to be forwarded by the MCP client during the discovery phase
user_stories.value: discovery completes successfully without 403 errors, and I do not need an out-of-band workaround to authenticate

user_stories.persona: a security engineer auditing a LangChain-based service
user_stories.action: rely on validate_safe_url to block attacker-controlled hostnames unconditionally, regardless of the LANGCHAIN_ENV environment variable value
user_stories.value: SSRF protections cannot be silently disabled by environment variable manipulation in production or staging deployments

user_stories.persona: an enterprise engineer needing uniform transport security across all LangChain provider integrations
user_stories.action: configure custom httpx clients consistently across ChatAnthropic and AzureChatOpenAI using the same interface pattern
user_stories.value: I do not need provider-specific workarounds; one mental model covers all integrations

acceptance_criteria.given: a developer constructs a ChatAnthropic instance with a custom httpx.Client or httpx.AsyncClient passed as a parameter
acceptance_criteria.when: the integration makes any outbound request
acceptance_criteria.then: the custom client — including its TLS configuration, certificate settings, and proxy settings — is used for that request, with no fallback to a default client

acceptance_criteria.given: a developer constructs an AzureChatOpenAI instance with a shared httpx client passed as a parameter
acceptance_criteria.when: multiple AzureChatOpenAI instances are created with the same client object
acceptance_criteria.then: no additional connection pools are created; all instances route through the provided shared client

acceptance_criteria.given: an MCP client is configured with an Authorization header and connects to a remote MCP server
acceptance_criteria.then: the Authorization header is included in all discovery-phase HTTP requests, and a valid response is received from a server that requires that header

acceptance_criteria.given: LANGCHAIN_ENV is set to local_test in the runtime environment
acceptance_criteria.when: validate_safe_url is called with a hostname that would otherwise be blocked by SSRF rules
acceptance_criteria.then: the URL is still blocked and a validation error is raised, identical to behavior when LANGCHAIN_ENV is unset or set to any other value

acceptance_criteria.given: validate_safe_url is called with an attacker-controlled hostname (e.g., an internal IP or reserved address)
acceptance_criteria.when: any value of LANGCHAIN_ENV is present
acceptance_criteria.then: the function raises a validation error and does not make any outbound request to that hostname

acceptance_criteria.given: a custom httpx client is injected into ChatAnthropic with a client-level timeout configuration
acceptance_criteria.when: a request times out according to the custom client's settings
acceptance_criteria.then: the timeout error is surfaced to the caller without the integration overriding the client's timeout with a default value

acceptance_criteria.given: a developer does not supply a custom httpx client to ChatAnthropic or AzureChatOpenAI
acceptance_criteria.then: behavior is identical to the current default — no regression in out-of-the-box usage

acceptance_criteria.given: an MCP client is configured without any Authorization header
acceptance_criteria.when: the discovery phase is executed against a public MCP server
acceptance_criteria.then: discovery completes successfully and no Authorization header is injected — confirming the forwarding is additive and not destructive to unauthenticated flows

success_metrics.target: 0 new issues of this type within 60 days of release

success_metrics.definition: Count of reported instances of 403 errors during MCP discovery attributable to missing Authorization header forwarding

success_metrics.name: SSRF bypass regression
success_metrics.definition: Count of security reports or test failures demonstrating that validate_safe_url can be bypassed via any environment variable value
success_metrics.target: 0 reports in any post-release security audit or automated test run

success_metrics.name: Integration test coverage for secure transport
success_metrics.definition: Count of automated integration tests covering custom httpx client injection (ChatAnthropic and AzureChatOpenAI), MCP Authorization header forwarding, and SSRF validation under all LANGCHAIN_ENV values
success_metrics.target: At least 6 net-new automated tests merged alongside the feature work

out_of_scope: OAuth 2.0 or token-refresh lifecycle management within LangChain integrations
Custom httpx client support for providers other than ChatAnthropic and AzureChatOpenAI in this iteration
MCP server-side authentication implementation or MCP server hardening
General proxy auto-discovery or PAC file support
User-facing documentation or developer portal changes (tracked separately)
Secrets management or credential rotation infrastructure
Rate limiting or request throttling tied to client identity

risks.description: The SSRF bypass via LANGCHAIN_ENV=local_test is a security vulnerability. If this PRD is not prioritized and shipped promptly, any deployment where that variable is set or can be influenced by an attacker is exposed. The fix should be treated as a security patch independent of the broader feature work if timelines diverge.

Introducing a custom httpx client parameter to ChatAnthropic and AzureChatOpenAI risks breaking existing subclasses or integrations that override internal client construction. A careful deprecation path and backward-compatibility contract must be defined before release.

Pain points 2, 3, and 4 each have a frequency of 1 in the underlying evidence, meaning they are supported by a single observed issue each. The true prevalence in the user base may be higher (silent failures, undisclosed enterprise deployments) or these may be edge cases. Shipping all four fixes together as a coherent 'secure transport' initiative is justified, but the business impact case for items 2 and 3 specifically rests on thin public evidence.

MCP header forwarding changes must not inadvertently forward Authorization headers to unintended third-party endpoints if an MCP discovery response redirects to a different host. A host-scoping guard must be implemented alongside the forwarding feature to prevent credential leakage.

Shared httpx client injection in AzureChatOpenAI may conflict with Azure SDK's own internal client management or retry logic, requiring deeper integration work than a surface-level parameter addition.
